A particle of mass m starts sliding down from rest from the endpoint P of the track. When it slides to the lowest point Q, its normal pressure on the track is 2mg, and the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration is g. During the process in which the particle slides from P to Q, the work done in overcoming friction is (　　)

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: As shown in the figure, a semicircular track of radius R is fixed vertically, and the two ends of the track are at the same height. A particle of mass m starts sliding down from rest from the endpoint P of the track. When it slides to the lowest point Q, its normal pressure on the track is 2mg, and the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration is g. Find the work done in overcoming friction during the process in which the particle slides from P to Q.
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure, there is a vertically placed semicircular track, with the semicircle opening upward, and the lowest point is marked as Q. At the left endpoint there is the particle position P; P and the center of the circle O are located at the height of the same horizontal dashed line; the right endpoint is also near the height of this dashed line. In the figure, a radius is drawn from O to the lower right of the track, marked as R. Therefore, the vertical descending height from P to the lowest point Q is R. Then reason: When the particle reaches point Q, the problem states that the particle's normal pressure on the track is 2mg, so the magnitude of the supporting force of the track on the particle is also N=2mg, and its direction at the lowest point points toward the center of the circle, that is, vertically upward. Gravity mg is vertically downward. Write the centripetal force equation along the radial direction: N-mg=\frac{mv_Q^2}{R}. Substitute N=2mg to get 2mg-mg=\frac{mv_Q^2}{R}, so v_Q^2=gR. Use the kinetic energy theorem from P to Q. Point P starts from rest, and the initial kinetic energy is 0; the kinetic energy at point Q is \frac12 mv_Q^2=\frac12 mgR. The work done by gravity is mgR, the supporting force does no work, and friction does negative work. Let the work done in overcoming friction be W, then the work done by friction is -W. Thus mgR-W=\frac12 mgR, solving gives W=\frac12 mgR. Final answer: \frac12 mgR.
